title: Unifying Intuition and Scientific Discovery: From Category Redrawing to Drug–Probe Unity and Toxicant–Probe Unity
content: Scientific discovery repeatedly involves a judgment that precedes formal argument: certain dichotomies entrenched by disciplinary institutions may be epistemological conveniences rather than ontological ruptures. This article calls this judgment “unifying intuition” and distinguishes two operations. The deconstructive operation removes a boundary treated as a premise; the elevating operation introduces a deeper category that subsumes older categories as special cases. Both are disciplined by the same requirement: a formal system must be built, must bear falsifiable empirical risk, and must be willing to demarcate its own domain of failure. The article first traces the philosophical genealogy of this intuition—from Plato’s one and many, Spinoza’s attribute monism, Kant’s transcendental unity of apperception, and Hegel’s Aufhebung, to Quine’s ontological commitment and Davidson’s critique of conceptual schemes—and distinguishes it from Whewell’s “consilience,” Thaliath’s “structural intuition,” and Duhem’s position that unification is “intuited rather than deduced.” It then surveys cross-disciplinary cases. Wöhler’s dissolution of the organic–inorganic boundary, Darwin’s redrawing of the human–animal boundary, Newton’s unification of celestial and terrestrial motion, and Einstein’s dissolution of absolute simultaneity, of the inertia–gravitation dichotomy, and of the mass–energy dichotomy exemplifies the deconstructive mode. Maxwell’s unification of electricity, magnetism, and light; Yang–Mills theory’s elevation of local symmetry over force; electroweak unification and the Standard Model; Landau’s symmetry-breaking account of phase transitions; BCS theory; Mendeleev’s periodic classification; Dirac’s unification of quantum mechanics and special relativity; statistical mechanics; and the first law of thermodynamics exemplify the elevating mode. Cases from Leibniz, Shannon, Wegener, Freud, Wiener, and Bohr demonstrate that the structure is not confined to physics. The article then turns to two contemporary redrawings in pharmacology and toxicology. Drug–Probe Unity (DPU) recasts therapy and imaging from an external combination of modules into two facets of one molecular entity, formalized through the ACQ/AIE/ARE/ARN four-state taxonomy and a triple unity of pharmacophore–fluorophore, drug–probe, and drug–praxis. Toxicant–Probe Unity (TPU) rejects the separation assumption that the toxicant is silent and the probe external, arguing that for intrinsically fluorescent toxicants, aggregation-state photophysics can serve as a state readout of distribution, biotransformation, and target engagement, connected to AOP, NAM, and QST frameworks through a triple unity of toxicophore–fluorophore, toxicant–probe, and toxicant–practice. The article concludes that the value of DPU and TPU lies not in conceptual comprehensiveness but in testable predictions and explicit boundary conditions such as ARN. The framework’s scientific weight will be decided by whether independent laboratories adopt it as a working hypothesis and whether its central predictions survive empirical testing.
